title: Generative Frontier Planning for Adaptive Peer-Referral Recruitment under Covariate-Dependent Arrivals

paper.title: Generative Frontier Planning for Adaptive Peer-Referral Recruitment under Covariate-Dependent Arrivals
paper.abstract:
Abstract. Peer-referral recruitment systems such as respondent-driven sampling are
critical for studying and intervening on hidden populations affected by
infectious diseases. To accelerate recruitment, public health agencies must
adaptively allocate limited referral resources across multiple rounds, where
current decisions shape both the number and the covariates of future
recruits. Prior work makes this problem tractable by assuming that referrals
are drawn i.i.d. from a homogeneous population, an assumption that ignores
the homophily and shared context that drive real peer recruitment. We
instead consider a more realistic model in which both referral capacity and
the covariates of newly referred individuals are conditioned on the
referrer, learned from data with a censored count model and a conditional
generative model. The
resulting planning problem is challenging because each candidate allocation
induces a different distribution over future recruits. We propose Generative Frontier Planning (GFP), a model-based planner
that replaces per-step Monte-Carlo sampling with a deterministic backup
over a latent covariate-coverage value surrogate. The surrogate is designed
so that the expected value of the next frontier depends on the offspring generative model only through finite-dimensional summaries that are amortized offline, and so that the resulting per-round objective is
monotone with diminishing returns. Together, these two properties make
planning tractable: the deterministic backup eliminates Monte-Carlo
sampling, and the diminishing-returns structure lets a marginal greedy
allocation achieve a ( 1 − 1 / e ) (1-1/e) -approximation for the per-round problem.
On a simulation environment calibrated to a real respondent-driven sampling
dataset, GFP outperforms random, reinforcement-learning, and i.i.d. dynamic-programming baselines across four discount factors.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text: Peer-referral recruitment systems such as respondent-driven sampling (RDS) ( Goel and Salganik, 2009 ) and incentivized contact tracing ( Munzert et al., 2021 ) are crucial tools for studying and preventing the spread of infectious diseases. In these settings, enrolled individuals recursively refer their peers into the study, enabling public health agencies to learn about behavior, disease prevalence, and population structure—especially in “hidden” populations that are otherwise largely unobserved and underserved ( Heckathorn, 1997 ) . The resulting recruitment data are also valuable for informing downstream decisions about limited intervention resources ( Kangaslahti et al., 2026 ; Chen and Lu, 2017 ) . To encourage participation, public health agencies distribute limited resources, such as referral vouchers or monetary incentives, to enrolled individuals. Because peer recruitment unfolds recursively over time, the decision-maker can split a fixed total budget into multiple rounds, adapting to the observed “frontier” of active recruits as recruitment proceeds. Individuals themselves also act adaptively: the number of peers they refer can depend on the amount of resources they receive. Public health agencies must therefore design adaptive allocation strategies that reason about complex referral dynamics in order to recruit as many individuals as possible as quickly as possible. Although this problem has been studied in prior work ( Pan et al., 2026 ) , that formulation assumes that referrals for newly recruited individuals are drawn i.i.d. from a fixed population-level distribution. Under this assumption, the value of a recruitment frontier depends only on its size. This is mathematically convenient but ignores dependence between referrers and their referees, which is unrealistic in practice: peer referrals are shaped by homophily, geographic proximity, and shared behavioral context. We address this limitation with a more realistic data-driven model in which referral dynamics are conditioned on referrer covariates, drawing on recent generative models of infectious-disease recruitment ( Kangaslahti et al., 2026 ) . 1 Observe current active frontier At round t t , observe the current active referrers (frontier) and remaining budget r t r_{t} . Under this modeling shift, planning becomes substantially more challenging. The value of a frontier now depends not only on its size but also on its covariate composition, so prior allocation algorithms that summarize a frontier by frontier size alone become suboptimal. Beyond this, model-based planning faces two coupled obstacles. First, computing the expected value of the next frontier has no closed form: the next frontier is a variable-size random set whose elements are drawn from a generative offspring model, so the expectation must in principle be estimated by Monte-Carlo sampling. Second, since different allocations induce different offspring distributions, these samples cannot be shared across candidate allocations, and the per-round action space (integer allocations across all frontier individuals) is itself combinatorially large. Together, these obstacles make naive model-based planning intractable. In this work, we propose a model-based planning method that addresses both obstacles. We learn referral dynamics with a censored count model and a conditional diffusion model of offspring covariates, and combine them with a budget-conditioned value surrogate over latent covariate coverage. The surrogate is designed so that two properties hold simultaneously. First, its expected future value depends on the diffusion model only through finite-dimensional summaries of the offspring distribution (the conditional Laplace embeddings) that are amortized offline; the resulting Bellman backup is fully deterministic and shared across candidate allocations, eliminating per-step Monte-Carlo sampling. Second, the induced per-round objective is monotone with diminishing returns, so a marginal greedy allocation achieves a ( 1 − 1 / e ) (1-1/e) -approximation despite the combinatorial action space. We summarize our contributions as follows: (1) We formalize peer-referral recruitment as adaptive multi-round resource allocation in which both the number and the covariates of future arrivals are generated conditional on the current allocation and frontier, generalizing prior i.i.d. population-level formulations ( Pan et al., 2026 ) . (2) We propose Generative Frontier Planning (GFP), a model-based planner that combines a learned censored count model and a learned conditional diffusion model of offspring covariates with a latent-coverage value surrogate. Using conditional Laplace embeddings of the offspring model, GFP evaluates expected future values in closed form, replacing per-step Monte-Carlo sampling with a deterministic backup that is used identically for planning and fitted-value-iteration training. (3) We prove that the resulting surrogate is monotone with integer diminishing returns, giving a ( 1 − 1 / e ) (1-1/e) -approximation guarantee for the per-round allocation. Empirically, on a simulation environment calibrated to a real respondent-driven sampling dataset, GFP outperforms random allocation, reinforcement learning baselines, and an i.i.d. population-level dynamic-programming baseline across four discount factors.

sections.heading: 2. Problem Formulation
sections.text: We formulate adaptive multi-round peer-referral recruitment as a finite-horizon planning problem with a total budget B B allocated across rounds. We use t = 0 , 1 , 2 , … t=0,1,2,\ldots to index rounds and suppress the round index when describing the per-round mechanics below; subscripts in t t reappear only in the multi-round objective.

sections.heading: State and action.
sections.text: At the current round, the decision-maker observes a frontier of active individuals ℱ = { 𝐱 1 , … , 𝐱 n } , \mathcal{F}=\{\mathbf{x}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{n}\}, where 𝐱 i ∈ 𝒳 \mathbf{x}_{i}\in\mathcal{X} denotes the covariate vector of individual i i (e.g., demographic, behavioral, geographic, or network features) and the frontier size n = | ℱ | n=|\mathcal{F}| varies across rounds. The remaining budget r ∈ ℕ 0 r\in\mathbb{N}_{0} is initialized to r 0 = B r_{0}=B , where ℕ 0 = { 0 , 1 , 2 , … } \mathbb{N}_{0}=\{0,1,2,\ldots\} . An action consists of a round budget s ∈ { 0 , … , r } s\in\{0,\ldots,r\} and an integer allocation vector 𝐤 = ( k 1 , … , k n ) ∈ ℕ 0 n , ∑ i = 1 n k i = s , \mathbf{k}=(k_{1},\ldots,k_{n})\in\mathbb{N}_{0}^{n},\qquad\sum_{i=1}^{n}k_{i}=s, where k i k_{i} is the number of referral resources assigned to individual i i ; the case s = 0 s=0 corresponds to assigning no resources in the current round.

sections.text: Each frontier individual i i has a stochastic referral capacity C i ∼ q ⋆ ( ⋅ ∣ 𝐱 i ) , C_{i}\sim q^{\star}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{x}_{i}), where q ⋆ q^{\star} is an unknown conditional count distribution. Given allocation k i k_{i} , the realized number of successful referrals is the capped count N i ​ ( k i ) = min ⁡ { k i , C i } . N_{i}(k_{i})=\min\{k_{i},C_{i}\}. The immediate reward in the current round is therefore R ⁡ ( ℱ , 𝐤 , C ) = ∑ i = 1 n N i ​ ( k i ) , C = ( C 1 , … , C n ) . R(\mathcal{F},\mathbf{k};C)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}N_{i}(k_{i}),\qquad C=(C_{1},\ldots,C_{n}). Because each individual’s output is capped at the realized capacity C i C_{i} , any units assigned beyond C i C_{i} are wasted; equivalently, the expected per-unit yield Pr C ∼ q ⋆ ( ⋅ ∣ 𝐱 i ) ( C ≥ ℓ ) \Pr_{C\sim q^{\star}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{x}_{i})}(C\geq\ell) is nonincreasing in ℓ \ell .

sections.heading: Covariate-dependent generative arrivals.
sections.text: In contrast to population-level arrival models in which newly referred individuals are sampled i.i.d. from a fixed population distribution, we assume that offspring covariates depend on the referrer. Conditional on N i ​ ( k i ) N_{i}(k_{i}) , the covariates of individual i i ’s referrals are drawn as 𝐱 i ​ j ′ ∼ G ⋆ ( ⋅ ∣ 𝐱 i ) , j = 1 , … , N i ( k i ) , \mathbf{x}^{\prime}_{ij}\sim G^{\star}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{x}_{i}),\qquad j=1,\ldots,N_{i}(k_{i}), where G ⋆ G^{\star} is an unknown parent-conditioned offspring covariate distribution. The next frontier is the random set ℱ ′ = { 𝐱 i ​ j ′ : i ∈ { 1 , … , n } , j = 1 , … , N i ( k i ) } . \mathcal{F}^{\prime}=\bigl\{\mathbf{x}^{\prime}_{ij}:i\in\{1,\ldots,n\},\ j=1,\ldots,N_{i}(k_{i})\bigr\}. This captures the fact that referrals are not drawn from a homogeneous population: individuals tend to recruit others whose covariates are shaped by their own social, geographic, demographic, or behavioral context.

sections.heading: Policy and objective.
sections.text: A policy π \pi maps each state ( r , ℱ ) (r,\mathcal{F}) to a feasible action ( s , 𝐤 ) (s,\mathbf{k}) . sections.heading: 3. Proposed Method
sections.text: We propose Generative Frontier Planning (GFP), a model-based approximate dynamic programming method for adaptive multi-round allocation under covariate-dependent arrivals. The method proceeds in three steps. Section 3.1 introduces the learned referral dynamics and explains why generic model-based fitted value iteration is intractable. Section 3.2 introduces a structured value surrogate whose Bellman backup admits a closed-form expression through conditional Laplace embeddings of the offspring distribution. Section 3.3 describes intra-round greedy allocation under the resulting deterministic surrogate and gives the fixed-budget approximation guarantee. Section 3.4 describes how the surrogate is fitted using the same closed-form backup.

sections.heading: 3.1. Model-Based Value Fitting and Its Computational Bottleneck
sections.text: GFP is a model-based planner: the true dynamics q ⋆ q^{\star} and G ⋆ G^{\star} are unknown, so we plan with learned surrogates q ψ q_{\psi} and G θ G_{\theta} estimated offline from historical referral data.

sections.heading: Learning referral dynamics.
sections.text: GFP uses two learned components: a conditional referral-capacity model q ψ ​ ( c ∣ 𝐱 ) ≈ q ⋆ ​ ( c ∣ 𝐱 ) q_{\psi}(c\mid\mathbf{x})\approx q^{\star}(c\mid\mathbf{x}) , and a conditional offspring covariate model G θ ​ ( 𝐱 ′ ∣ 𝐱 ) ≈ G ⋆ ​ ( 𝐱 ′ ∣ 𝐱 ) G_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\mid\mathbf{x})\approx G^{\star}(\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\mid\mathbf{x}) . The first models the stochastic referral capacity C i C_{i} of an individual with covariates 𝐱 i \mathbf{x}_{i} . In referral systems, the observed number of successful referrals is censored by the allocated budget: if individual i i receives k i k_{i} resources and generates y i y_{i} successful referrals, then y i = min ⁡ { C i , k i } y_{i}=\min\{C_{i},k_{i}\} . We therefore fit q ψ q_{\psi} under the censored likelihood ℙ ⁡ ( Y i = y i ∣ 𝐱 i , k i ) = { q ψ ​ ( y i ∣ 𝐱 i ) , y i < k i , ℙ C ∼ q ψ ( ⋅ ∣ 𝐱 i ) ( C ≥ k i ) , y i = k i , \mathbb{P}(Y_{i}=y_{i}\mid\mathbf{x}_{i},k_{i})=\begin{cases}q_{\psi}(y_{i}\mid\mathbf{x}_{i}),&y_{i}<k_{i},\\ \mathbb{P}_{C\sim q_{\psi}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{x}_{i})}(C\geq k_{i}),&y_{i}=k_{i},\end{cases} which avoids treating saturated observations y i = k i y_{i}=k_{i} as evidence that the true capacity equals k i k_{i} . In our implementation, q ψ q_{\psi} is a neural Poisson regression model whose rate depends on the parent covariates. The second models the covariates of newly referred individuals. Given a parent covariate vector 𝐱 \mathbf{x} , the offspring covariate vector 𝐱 ′ \mathbf{x}^{\prime} is drawn from G θ ( ⋅ ∣ 𝐱 ) G_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{x}) . We instantiate G θ G_{\theta} as a conditional diffusion model ( Ho et al., 2020 ) over the covariate space 𝒳 \mathcal{X} , which provides a flexible generative model for high-dimensional covariates. Other conditional generative models (e.g., conditional normalizing flows ( Winkler et al., 2019 ) ) could be substituted without changing the rest of the framework.

The immediate-reward term A ψ ​ ( ℱ , 𝐤 ) A_{\psi}(\mathcal{F},\mathbf{k}) decomposes additively over individuals and is closed form: p ψ , i ​ ( ℓ ) p_{\psi,i}(\ell) is the probability that the ℓ \ell -th unit assigned to individual i i is not wasted. The expected-future-value term, by contrast, is intractable. Computing the Bellman backup faces three coupled challenges: (C1) Random next frontier. For a generic V ϕ V_{\phi} , the expected future value 𝔼 ⁡ [ V ϕ ​ ( r − s , ℱ ′ ) ] \mathbb{E}[V_{\phi}(r-s,\mathcal{F}^{\prime})] has no closed form: ℱ ′ \mathcal{F}^{\prime} is a random set whose size depends on 𝐤 \mathbf{k} through q ψ q_{\psi} , and whose elements are drawn from the diffusion model G θ G_{\theta} . A Monte-Carlo estimator must sample ℱ ′ \mathcal{F}^{\prime} and evaluate V ϕ V_{\phi} on the sampled set. (C2) Combinatorial action space. For each candidate round budget s s , there are ( s + n − 1 n − 1 ) \binom{s+n-1}{n-1} feasible integer allocations, which is prohibitive for the frontier sizes and budgets we consider. (C3) Allocation–expectation coupling. Different allocations 𝐤 \mathbf{k} induce different next-frontier distributions, so the Monte-Carlo estimate in (C1) cannot be shared across the action space in (C2): each candidate 𝐤 \mathbf{k} requires its own offspring samples. Together, (C1)–(C3) make generic Monte-Carlo fitted value iteration intractable. We resolve all three by choosing a structured value surrogate whose expected future value is a deterministic function of finite-dimensional amortized summaries of G θ G_{\theta} , and whose induced fixed-budget objective is monotone with diminishing returns.

sections.heading: 3.2. Structured Value Surrogate and Closed-Form Backup
sections.text: We restrict V ϕ V_{\phi} to a structured form that has two key properties: (i) given offline-amortized summaries of G θ G_{\theta} and q ψ q_{\psi} , the expected future value 𝔼 ⁡ [ V ϕ ​ ( r − s , ℱ ′ ) ] \mathbb{E}[V_{\phi}(r-s,\mathcal{F}^{\prime})] is a deterministic function of 𝐤 \mathbf{k} , so no per-step Monte-Carlo sampling is required and the same amortized summaries serve every candidate allocation; and (ii) the induced per-round objective is monotone with diminishing returns, which we exploit in Section 3.3 to obtain a ( 1 − 1 / e ) (1-1/e) -approximation via marginal greedy allocation. Property (i) addresses (C1) and (C3); property (ii) addresses (C2). We develop property (i) in this section.

sections.heading: Adaptive multi-round allocation and budgeted MDPs.
sections.text: Most closely related to our setting is adaptive multi-round allocation with stochastic arrivals ( Pan et al., 2026 ) , which obtains tractability by assuming i.i.d. population-level future arrivals and summarizing the frontier by its size alone, so that the value function reduces to a table over remaining budget and frontier size. Our method generalizes this framework to covariate-dependent generative arrivals, where the next frontier is drawn conditional on the referrer, and future value therefore depends on covariate composition rather than only on frontier size. More broadly, resource-constrained sequential decision problems are commonly modeled by constrained or budgeted MDPs ( Boutilier and Lu, 2016 ; Carrara et al., 2019 ) , and large-scale allocation settings with weakly coupled subprocesses motivate decomposition-based planning rather than direct dynamic programming over the full joint state ( Meuleau et al., 1998 ; Dolgov and Durfee, 2005 ) . These formulations typically assume a fixed set of controlled entities; in our setting, allocating resources to the current frontier changes the future set of decision opportunities, resembling a controlled branching process. Branching MDPs formalize such controlled population growth but mainly target extinction or reachability over finite-type populations, rather than budgeted allocation over covariate-composed frontiers ( Etessami et al., 2019 ) .

sections.heading: Approximate dynamic programming for stochastic allocation.
sections.text: When exact Bellman recursions are ruled out by high-dimensional state spaces, large action sets, or stochastic future arrivals, a common strategy is approximate dynamic programming ( Powell, 2007 ; Bertsekas, 2012 ; Bertsekas, 2025 ; Fadaki et al., 2025 ) , in which the value function is replaced by a tractable parametric or aggregated surrogate. Classical surrogates include feature-based value approximation ( Tsitsiklis and Van Roy, 1996 ) and attribute-level state aggregation in resource allocation ( George et al., 2008 ) , where the state is compressed into a low-dimensional summary that preserves enough information about future value to guide present decisions. Our structured surrogate fits within this lineage but is designed for allocation-dependent frontier growth: instead of compressing the frontier into a scalar size, it embeds each frontier individual into a nonnegative latent coverage vector and values the frontier by its aggregate coverage, which is what enables the closed-form Bellman backup of Section 3 .

sections.heading: Submodular optimization and greedy approximation.
sections.text: Our per-round guarantee draws on submodular maximization, which provides a classical framework for reasoning about diminishing returns in allocation and coverage problems. For monotone submodular maximization under a cardinality constraint, the greedy algorithm achieves the tight ( 1 − 1 / e ) (1-1/e) -approximation ( Nemhauser et al., 1978 ) . Adaptive submodularity further extends greedy guarantees to sequential decisions with uncertain outcomes ( Golovin and Krause, 2011 ) . Our method exploits this perspective through a coverage-based future-value surrogate: for each fixed round budget, the surrogate objective is monotone with diminishing returns, yielding a ( 1 − 1 / e ) (1-1/e) -approximation for the intra-round allocation; cross-round adaptivity is handled separately through the budget-conditioned future-value surrogate rather than by assuming adaptive submodularity of the full recruitment process.

sections.heading: 5. Experiments
sections.text: We evaluate GFP on a calibrated simulation environment designed to mirror real-world respondent-driven sampling. Section 5.1 introduces the simulation environment, calibrated to real-world public health dataset. Section 5.2 describes the four baselines we compare against. Section 5.3 specifies the episode protocol and evaluation metrics. Section 5.4 reports the empirical results.

sections.heading: 5.1. Calibrated Simulation Environment
sections.text: We evaluate all methods in a simulation environment whose structure mirrors real-world respondent-driven sampling. The environment’s covariate schema and inheritance probabilities are calibrated to the ICPSR 22140 respondent-driven sampling dataset, while the referral-capacity model is a parametric oracle. Each individual is represented by a d = 72 d=72 -dimensional one-hot covariate vector composed of K = 17 K=17 categorical fields (demographic, behavioral, and socioeconomic attributes) derived from the ICPSR 22140 schema ( Morris and Rothenberg, 2011 ) . The oracle referral-capacity model is a Poisson model with covariate-dependent rates, calibrated so that the expected per-individual capacity matches an average degree λ ¯ = 2.5 \bar{\lambda}=2.5 , with a 5 5 – 10 × 10\times spread between the highest- and lowest-rate individuals so that uniform allocation is substantially suboptimal. The oracle covariate transition model is a categorical inheritance kernel: for each of the K K covariate groups, the child independently inherits the parent’s category with a group-specific probability p k p_{k} (estimated from 73,669 73{,}669 recruiter–recruit dyads in ICPSR 22140; values range from p Sex = 0.22 p_{\textsc{Sex}}=0.22 to p Drugman = 0.98 p_{\textsc{Drugman}}=0.98 ), or is drawn uniformly otherwise. At the start of each episode the initial frontier ℱ 0 \mathcal{F}_{0} is sampled uniformly with replacement from a pre-generated pool of N = 300 N=300 random one-hot covariate vectors, with | ℱ 0 | = 10 |\mathcal{F}_{0}|=10 . Full schema definitions, the inheritance-probability estimator, and all parametric details are deferred to Appendix C.1 .

sections.heading: 5.2. Baselines
sections.text: We compare GFP against four baselines spanning random, reinforcement learning, and model-based dynamic-programming approaches.

sections.heading: Random.
sections.text: An unlearned baseline. At each round, it samples a round budget s t s_{t} uniformly from { 0 , … , b t } \{0,\dots,b_{t}\} and distributes the s t s_{t} units across frontier nodes by a single uniform multinomial draw.

sections.heading: Budget-DQN
sections.text: A RL method that learns only the round-level spending decision. A Q-network scores each feasible round budget given the current state; the selected budget is then split across frontier individuals by a fixed greedy allocator that prioritizes individuals with higher predicted recruitment counts. The budget decision and the individual-level allocation are decoupled.

sections.heading: Factorized RL
sections.text: A RL method that factorizes the combinatorial allocation action into three learned decisions: (i) how much budget to spend, (ii) how many individuals to activate, and (iii) how to score each candidate individual. A DeepSets encoder maps the variable-size frontier into a fixed-dimensional state; a three-head Q-network produces budget Q-values, k k -selection Q-values, and individual scores. At inference, the method selects the highest-value budget and k k , picks the top- k k individuals by score, and distributes the budget via softmax allocation with integer rounding.

sections.heading: IID-Population DP
sections.text: The model-based population-level method of ( Pan et al., 2026 ) . It approximates future value using only the remaining budget and frontier size, fit by backward induction over a (budget, frontier size) table on top of a marginal Poisson PMF estimated from covariate samples drawn from the planning pool. Future value is therefore based on the number of future recruits but not their covariate composition.

sections.heading: 5.3. Setup
sections.text: The simulation environment defines the ground-truth dynamics, but planning algorithms do not have direct access to the oracle models at test time. Instead, learning-based methods are trained against learned surrogates q ψ q_{\psi} and G θ G_{\theta} (the planning environment ), while final evaluation is conducted under the oracle dynamics q ⋆ , G ⋆ q^{\star},G^{\star} (the testing environment ). This separation ensures that performance comparisons are not confounded by differences in model fit. Full training data generation, model architectures, and hyperparameters are given in Appendix C.2 .

sections.heading: Episode protocol.
sections.text: Each episode starts with | ℱ 0 | = 10 |\mathcal{F}_{0}|=10 , a total budget B = 100 B=100 , and a maximum horizon of 50 50 rounds. Episodes terminate early if the budget is exhausted or the frontier becomes empty. We evaluate across four discount factors γ ∈ { 0.9 , 0.95 , 0.99 , 1.0 } \gamma\in\{0.9,\,0.95,\,0.99,\,1.0\} . sections.heading: Covariate composition matters.
sections.text: IID-Population DP is the strongest baseline because it shares two design choices with GFP—budget-level dynamic programming and a frontier-value surrogate—but summarizes the frontier by its size alone. The residual gap between GFP and IID-Population DP ( 8.2 8.2 recruits at γ = 1.0 \gamma=1.0 , 6.0 6.0 at γ = 0.9 \gamma=0.9 ) therefore isolates the value of reasoning about covariate composition under covariate-dependent arrivals.

sections.heading: RL baselines underperform.
sections.text: Both RL baselines lag behind GFP and IID-Population DP because they do not exploit the structure of the problem and must learn from reward signal alone over a combinatorial action space, which is too large to explore effectively. Factorized RL narrows the gap at high γ \gamma ( 90.3 90.3 at γ = 1.0 \gamma=1.0 ) by factorizing the action, but still degrades at low γ \gamma ( 57.9 57.9 at γ = 0.9 \gamma=0.9 ); Budget-DQN further decouples the budget decision from individual-level allocation and underperforms across all γ \gamma .

sections.heading: Early speed does not predict final performance.
sections.text: Figure 2 shows that GFP is not the fastest method in early rounds: at γ = 1.0 \gamma=1.0 , IID-Population DP reaches ≈ 90 \approx 90 recruits within 4 4 rounds and Factorized RL also rises quickly, while GFP advances more deliberately and overtakes both methods only in later rounds. Methods that front-load recruitment can plateau below methods that pace their allocation, so the first-few-round ranking reverses by the end. GFP’s advantage comes from covariate-aware allocation: it matches units to covariate-conditioned referral capacity and prioritizes individuals whose offspring expand the frontier into less-covered regions of latent coverage space. IID-Population DP shares GFP’s budget-level dynamic programming but summarizes the frontier by size alone, and so cannot make either decision. Random allocation plateaus near 39.4 39.4 across all γ \gamma , confirming that allocation strategy, not budget size, is the dominant driver of recruitment.

sections.heading: 6. Conclusion and Limitations
sections.text: We studied adaptive multi-round allocation for peer-referral recruitment in respondent-driven sampling, where allocation decisions shape both immediate rewards and the covariate composition of future frontiers. We proposed Generative Frontier Planning (GFP), a model-based planner that combines a censored count model and a conditional diffusion model of offspring covariates with a latent coverage value surrogate. Under this surrogate, the expected future value depends on the diffusion model only through conditional Laplace embeddings of the offspring distribution that are amortized offline, yielding a deterministic Bellman backup; and the per-round objective is monotone with diminishing returns, giving a ( 1 − 1 / e ) (1-1/e) -approximation guarantee for the intra-round allocation. On a simulation environment calibrated to the ICPSR-22140 respondent-driven sampling dataset, GFP outperforms random, reinforcement-learning, and i.i.d. population-level dynamic-programming baselines across four discount factors, demonstrating its potential to extend the reach of peer-referral recruitment systems in public health.

sections.heading: Limitations.
sections.text: Our environment is calibrated to a real respondent-driven sampling dataset but is ultimately driven by a known oracle. Validating GFP on real recruitment data, ideally in partnership with a public health agency, is an important next step.

Peer-referral recruitment systems such as respondent-driven sampling are critical for studying and intervening on hidden populations affected by infectious diseases. To accelerate recruitment, public health agencies must adaptively allocate limited referral resources across multiple rounds, where current decisions shape both the number and the covariates of future recruits. Prior work makes this problem tractable by assuming that referrals are drawn i.i.d. from a homogeneous population, an assumption that ignores the homophily and shared context that drive real peer recruitment. We instead consider a more realistic model in which both referral capacity and the covariates of newly referred individuals are conditioned on the referrer, learned from data with a censored count model and a conditional generative model. The resulting planning problem is challenging because each candidate allocation induces a different distribution over future recruits. We propose Generative Frontier Planning (GFP), a model-based planner that replaces per-step Monte-Carlo sampling with a deterministic backup over a latent covariate-coverage value surrogate. The surrogate is designed so that the expected value of the next frontier depends on the offspring generative model only through finite-dimensional summaries that are amortized offline, and so that the resulting per-round objective is monotone with diminishing returns. Together, these two properties make planning tractable: the deterministic backup eliminates Monte-Carlo sampling, and the diminishing-returns structure lets a marginal greedy allocation achieve a ( 1 − 1 / e ) (1-1/e) -approximation for the per-round problem. On a simulation environment calibrated to a real respondent-driven sampling dataset, GFP outperforms random, reinforcement-learning, and i.i.d. dynamic-programming baselines across four discount factors. 1. Introduction Peer-referral recruitment systems such as respondent-driven sampling (RDS) ( Goel and Salganik, 2009 ) and incentivized contact tracing ( Munzert et al., 2021 ) are crucial tools for studying and preventing the spread of infectious diseases. In these settings, enrolled individuals recursively refer their peers into the study, enabling public health agencies to learn about behavior, disease prevalence, and population structure—especially in “hidden” populations that are otherwise largely unobserved and underserved ( Heckathorn, 1997 ) . The resulting recruitment data are also valuable for informing downstream decisions about limited intervention resources ( Kangaslahti et al., 2026 ; Chen and Lu, 2017 ) . To encourage participation, public health agencies distribute limited resources, such as referral vouchers or monetary incentives, to enrolled individuals. Because peer recruitment unfolds recursively over time, the decision-maker can split a fixed total budget into multiple rounds, adapting to the observed “frontier” of active recruits as recruitment proceeds. Individuals themselves also act adaptively: the number of peers they refer can depend on the amount of resources they receive. Public health agencies must therefore design adaptive allocation strategies that reason about complex referral dynamics in order to recruit as many individuals as possible as quickly as possible. Although this problem has been studied in prior work ( Pan et al., 2026 ) , that formulation assumes that referrals for newly recruited individuals are drawn i.i.d. from a fixed population-level distribution. Under this assumption, the value of a recruitment frontier depends only on its size. This is mathematically convenient but ignores dependence between referrers and their referees, which is unrealistic in practice: peer referrals are shaped by homophily, geographic proximity, and shared behavioral context. We address this limitation with a more realistic data-driven model in which referral dynamics are conditioned on referrer covariates, drawing on recent generative models of infectious-disease recruitment ( Kangaslahti et al., 2026 ) . 1 Observe current active frontier At round t t , observe the current active referrers (frontier) and remaining budget r t r_{t} . Under this modeling shift, planning becomes substantially more challenging. The value of a frontier now depends not only on its size but also on its covariate composition, so prior allocation algorithms that summarize a frontier by frontier size alone become suboptimal. Beyond this, model-based planning faces two coupled obstacles. First, computing the expected value of the next frontier has no closed form: the next frontier is a variable-size random set whose elements are drawn from a generative offspring model, so the expectation must in principle be estimated by Monte-Carlo sampling. Second, since different allocations induce different offspring distributions, these samples cannot be shared across candidate allocations, and the per-round action space (integer allocations across all frontier individuals) is itself combinatorially large. Together, these obstacles make naive model-based planning intractable. In this work, we propose a model-based planning method that addresses both obstacles. We learn referral dynamics with a censored count model and a conditional diffusion model of offspring covariates, and combine them with a budget-conditioned value surrogate over latent covariate coverage. The surrogate is designed so that two properties hold simultaneously. First, its expected future value depends on the diffusion model only through finite-dimensional summaries of the offspring distribution (the conditional Laplace embeddings) that are amortized offline; the resulting Bellman backup is fully deterministic and shared across candidate allocations, eliminating per-step Monte-Carlo sampling. Second, the induced per-round objective is monotone with diminishing returns, so a marginal greedy allocation achieves a ( 1 − 1 / e ) (1-1/e) -approximation despite the combinatorial action space. We summarize our contributions as follows: (1) We formalize peer-referral recruitment as adaptive multi-round resource allocation in which both the number and the covariates of future arrivals are generated conditional on the current allocation and frontier, generalizing prior i.i.d. population-level formulations ( Pan et al., 2026 ) . (2) We propose Generative Frontier Planning (GFP), a model-based planner that combines a learned censored count model and a learned conditional diffusion model of offspring covariates with a latent-coverage value surrogate. Using conditional Laplace embeddings of the offspring model, GFP evaluates expected future values in closed form, replacing per-step Monte-Carlo sampling with a deterministic backup that is used identically for planning and fitted-value-iteration training. (3) We prove that the resulting surrogate is monotone with integer diminishing returns, giving a ( 1 − 1 / e ) (1-1/e) -approximation guarantee for the per-round allocation. Empirically, on a simulation environment calibrated to a real respondent-driven sampling dataset, GFP outperforms random allocation, reinforcement learning baselines, and an i.i.d. population-level dynamic-programming baseline across four discount factors. 2. Problem Formulation We formulate adaptive multi-round peer-referral recruitment as a finite-horizon planning problem with a total budget B B allocated across rounds. We use t = 0 , 1 , 2 , … t=0,1,2,\ldots to index rounds and suppress the round index when describing the per-round mechanics below; subscripts in t t reappear only in the multi-round objective. At the current round, the decision-maker observes a frontier of active individuals ℱ = { 𝐱 1 , … , 𝐱 n } , \mathcal{F}=\{\mathbf{x}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{n}\}, where 𝐱 i ∈ 𝒳 \mathbf{x}_{i}\in\mathcal{X} denotes the covariate vector of individual i i (e.g., demographic, behavioral, geographic, or network features) and the frontier size n = | ℱ | n=|\mathcal{F}| varies across rounds. Proposed Method We propose Generative Frontier Planning (GFP), a model-based approximate dynamic programming method for adaptive multi-round allocation under covariate-dependent arrivals. The method proceeds in three steps. Section 3.1 introduces the learned referral dynamics and explains why generic model-based fitted value iteration is intractable. Section 3.2 introduces a structured value surrogate whose Bellman backup admits a closed-form expression through conditional Laplace embeddings of the offspring distribution. Section 3.3 describes intra-round greedy allocation under the resulting deterministic surrogate and gives the fixed-budget approximation guarantee. Section 3.4 describes how the surrogate is fitted using the same closed-form backup. 3.1. Model-Based Value Fitting and Its Computational Bottleneck GFP is a model-based planner: the true dynamics q ⋆ q^{\star} and G ⋆ G^{\star} are unknown, so we plan with learned surrogates q ψ q_{\psi} and G θ G_{\theta} estimated offline from historical referral data. Learning referral dynamics. GFP uses two learned components: a conditional referral-capacity model q ψ ​ ( c ∣ 𝐱 ) ≈ q ⋆ ​ ( c ∣ 𝐱 ) q_{\psi}(c\mid\mathbf{x})\approx q^{\star}(c\mid\mathbf{x}) , and a conditional offspring covariate model G θ ​ ( 𝐱 ′ ∣ 𝐱 ) ≈ G ⋆ ​ ( 𝐱 ′ ∣ 𝐱 ) G_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\mid\mathbf{x})\approx G^{\star}(\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\mid\mathbf{x}) . The first models the stochastic referral capacity C i C_{i} of an individual with covariates 𝐱 i \mathbf{x}_{i} . In referral systems, the observed number of successful referrals is censored by the allocated budget: if individual i i receives k i k_{i} resources and generates y i y_{i} successful referrals, then y i = min ⁡ { C i , k i } y_{i}=\min\{C_{i},k_{i}\} . Other conditional generative models (e.g., conditional normalizing flows ( Winkler et al., 2019 ) ) could be substituted without changing the rest of the framework. Generic model-based fitted value iteration. A natural way to use the learned models is fitted value iteration. Given a value function V ϕ ​ ( r , ℱ ) V_{\phi}(r,\mathcal{F}) , the model-based Bellman backup decomposes into an expected immediate reward and an expected future value: (1) ( 𝒯 V ϕ ) ( r , ℱ ) = max 0 ≤ s ≤ r max 𝐤 ∈ ℕ 0 n : ∑ i k i = s { A ψ ( ℱ , 𝐤 ) + γ 𝔼 [ V ϕ ( r − s , ℱ ′ ) ] } , (\mathcal{T}V_{\phi})(r,\mathcal{F})=\max_{0\leq s\leq r}\,\max_{\mathbf{k}\in\mathbb{N}_{0}^{n}:\,\sum_{i}k_{i}=s}\Bigl\{A_{\psi}(\mathcal{F},\mathbf{k})+\gamma\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[V_{\phi}(r-s,\mathcal{F}^{\prime})\right]\Bigr\}, where the expected immediate reward is (2) A ψ ​ ( ℱ , 𝐤 ) = ∑ i = 1 n ∑ ℓ = 1 k i p ψ , i ​ ( ℓ ) , A_{\psi}(\mathcal{F},\mathbf{k})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{\ell=1}^{k_{i}}p_{\psi,i}(\ell), with survival probability p ψ , i ( ℓ ) ≔ ℙ C ∼ q ψ ( ⋅ ∣ 𝐱 i ) ( C ≥ ℓ ) p_{\psi,i}(\ell)\coloneqq\mathbb{P}_{C\sim q_{\psi}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{x}_{i})}(C\geq\ell) , and the future-value expectation is over C i ∼ q ψ ( ⋅ ∣ 𝐱 i ) C_{i}\sim q_{\psi}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{x}_{i}) , N i = min ⁡ { k i , C i } N_{i}=\min\{k_{i},C_{i}\} , and offspring covariates 𝐱 i ​ j ′ ∼ G θ ( ⋅ ∣ 𝐱 i ) \mathbf{x}^{\prime}_{ij}\sim G_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{x}_{i}) forming the next frontier ℱ ′ = { 𝐱 i ​ j ′ : i = 1 , … , n , j = 1 , … , N i } \mathcal{F}^{\prime}=\{\mathbf{x}^{\prime}_{ij}:i=1,\ldots,n,\,j=1,\ldots,N_{i}\} . The expected-future-value term, by contrast, is intractable. Computing the Bellman backup faces three coupled challenges: (C1) Random next frontier. For a generic V ϕ V_{\phi} , the expected future value 𝔼 ⁡ [ V ϕ ​ ( r − s , ℱ ′ ) ] \mathbb{E}[V_{\phi}(r-s,\mathcal{F}^{\prime})] has no closed form: ℱ ′ \mathcal{F}^{\prime} is a random set whose size depends on 𝐤 \mathbf{k} through q ψ q_{\psi} , and whose elements are drawn from the diffusion model G θ G_{\theta} . A Monte-Carlo estimator must sample ℱ ′ \mathcal{F}^{\prime} and evaluate V ϕ V_{\phi} on the sampled set. (C2) Combinatorial action space. For each candidate round budget s s , there are ( s + n − 1 n − 1 ) \binom{s+n-1}{n-1} feasible integer allocations, which is prohibitive for the frontier sizes and budgets we consider. (C3) Allocation–expectation coupling. Different allocations 𝐤 \mathbf{k} induce different next-frontier distributions, so the Monte-Carlo estimate in (C1) cannot be shared across the action space in (C2): each candidate 𝐤 \mathbf{k} requires its own offspring samples. Related Work Adaptive multi-round allocation and budgeted MDPs. Most closely related to our setting is adaptive multi-round allocation with stochastic arrivals ( Pan et al., 2026 ) , which obtains tractability by assuming i.i.d. population-level future arrivals and summarizing the frontier by its size alone, so that the value function reduces to a table over remaining budget and frontier size. Our method generalizes this framework to covariate-dependent generative arrivals, where the next frontier is drawn conditional on the referrer, and future value therefore depends on covariate composition rather than only on frontier size. More broadly, resource-constrained sequential decision problems are commonly modeled by constrained or budgeted MDPs ( Boutilier and Lu, 2016 ; Carrara et al., 2019 ) , and large-scale allocation settings with weakly coupled subprocesses motivate decomposition-based planning rather than direct dynamic programming over the full joint state ( Meuleau et al., 1998 ; Dolgov and Durfee, 2005 ) . These formulations typically assume a fixed set of controlled entities; in our setting, allocating resources to the current frontier changes the future set of decision opportunities, resembling a controlled branching process. Branching MDPs formalize such controlled population growth but mainly target extinction or reachability over finite-type populations, rather than budgeted allocation over covariate-composed frontiers ( Etessami et al., 2019 ) . Approximate dynamic programming for stochastic allocation. When exact Bellman recursions are ruled out by high-dimensional state spaces, large action sets, or stochastic future arrivals, a common strategy is approximate dynamic programming ( Powell, 2007 ; Bertsekas, 2012 ; Bertsekas, 2025 ; Fadaki et al., 2025 ) , in which the value function is replaced by a tractable parametric or aggregated surrogate. Classical surrogates include feature-based value approximation ( Tsitsiklis and Van Roy, 1996 ) and attribute-level state aggregation in resource allocation ( George et al., 2008 ) , where the state is compressed into a low-dimensional summary that preserves enough information about future value to guide present decisions.
